articles.title: In 2025, a Virginia grandmother won $150,000 in the Powerball after asking ChatGPT for lottery numbers, then donated the entire prize to three charities close to her heart
articles.summary: In 2025, Carrie Edwards of Midlothian won the prize and gave every dollar of it to three charities.
articles.body: In 2025, Carrie Edwards of Midlothian won the prize and gave every dollar of it to three charities. Her story spread around the world after the Virginia Lottery publicised the gift. A retired public relations professional who rarely played, she says the decision to give the prize away came to her instantly. The causes she chose reflect her father’s naval career, her late husband’s illness and her volunteer work with a food-growing organisation in the Richmond area, and two of them received the money as demand for their services rose.How a friend’s lottery advice, an online ticket and ChatGPT led to a Powerball winAccording to The Washington Post, Edwards, who was 68 when the story was reported, walked into a 7-Eleven with a friend who wanted two Powerball tickets. The jackpot for the 6 September 2025 drawing had climbed above $1.7 billion, the second-largest ever. Edwards hardly ever played, and her friend, an active player, gave her two warnings, always buy a paper ticket, and never touch the Powerball multiplier because it is a scam. She ignored both.Instead, she created a Virginia Lottery account on her phone. Rather than relying on family birthdays or lucky numbers, she asked ChatGPT, which she had only recently started using for research, whether it had any winning numbers for her. The chatbot first replied that luck is luck, then supplied a set of numbers. She entered them and paid an extra dollar for the Power Play option.When she missed the huge jackpot, she assumed luck had not been on her side. She had not realised that she had chosen the option that re-enters the same numbers in the next drawing. A phone notification told her she had won, and she suspected a scam or a small prize of perhaps $10. Out of curiosity, she logged in and found she had matched four of the five numbers plus the Powerball, a $50,000 prize that the multiplier tripled.Why she decided within moments that the windfall was not hers to keep and where it should goAlone in her kitchen, Edwards was thunderstruck by the news. Almost at once, she said, she felt an overpowering conviction that the money was not hers. She resolved to give it all to her three most cherished charities.Her next thought was a joke at the expense of the friend whose advice she had ignored. He is an Army veteran, while she comes from a Navy family, so she privately gave the Navy the first point. Her three adult children were surprised by the win, and they supported her decision.How a naval family’s legacy sent money to military households as government pay worries grewEdwards is the daughter of a career naval officer. Her late father, a fighter pilot who ended his career in the office of the chief of naval operations at the Pentagon, asked in his will that his children donate part of their inheritance to the Navy-Marine Corps Relief Society. The non-profit provides financial assistance and other services to members of the military and their families.Her gift reached the society at a critical moment, according to its president and chief executive, Robert Ruark. Concerns were growing over government pay and furloughs as the federal government shut down at the end of September 2025. Ruark said the money was being used to help families facing hardship from the shutdown, deployments and everyday family emergencies.The husband’s illness behind a gift to dementia research and what the money was meant to fundHer late husband, Steve, inspired the second donation. In his late 50s, he was diagnosed with frontotemporal degeneration, the most common form of dementia in people under 60, which has no approved treatment to stop or slow it. As his condition worsened, Edwards retired from her public relations work to care for him. In 2023, the couple moved from Fairfax County in Northern Virginia to Midlothian, a Richmond suburb, so he could be closer to their children and new grandchildren. Steve died at the end of that year.After retiring, Edwards began volunteering for and giving to the Association for Frontotemporal Degeneration. Its chief executive, Susan Dickinson, said gifts range from $5 to more than $1 million, but the larger sums usually come from research partnerships and benefactors, so a single donation of Edwards’s size is rare. Dickinson described it as wonderfully impactful. The money was to go towards research, grants for pilot programmes, and bringing together people with the disease and those working on treatments.Why a food-growing organisation near Richmond saw her gift arrive just as demand surgedThe third beneficiary was Shalom Farms, where Edwards volunteered and served on the board when the story was reported. The non-profit grows fresh local produce and distributes it to about 10,000 Richmond residents. Her gift landed when the shutdown delayed food-assistance benefits, which drove a surge in demand.Executive Director Anna Ibrahim said the surprise donation let the farm buy more items so that it would have enough for everyone who came. The money was also to be invested across the organisation to support local farmers and other initiatives.Edwards told The Washington Post she had no regrets. She felt blessed to have been able to spread the word about causes she holds dear, and she hoped to inspire others. The attention, she said, gave her a platform to set an example for her children and to honour her husband’s and her father’s legacies through actions rather than words.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kent M20 crash involving 30 vehicles seriously injures two people
articles.summary: The crash happened in fog on Saturday evening on the London-bound carriageway near Maidstone, Kent.
articles.body:
More than 30 vehicles were involved in a crash which left two people seriously injured on the M20 in Kent on Saturday evening.

The crash happened in foggy conditions just after 18:40 GMT on the London-bound carriageway between junctions eight (Maidstone) and nine (Ashford).

Paramedics attended to 11 people, and two were taken to hospital, Kent Fire and Rescue Service said.

The road was shut in both directions early on Sunday, but has since reopened.

An air ambulance crew, three fire engines and a "technical rescue unit" were sent to the scene, where National Highways said "thick fog" had been confirmed.

Kent Police said one of the two people seriously injured had been taken to a hospital locally, and the other to a London hospital.

"Other drivers have sustained injuries not believed to be serious," it said in a statement.

The force has asked anyone with information about the incident or dashcam footage to come forward.

articles.title: DNA evidence revealed one brother was not the biological son of a millionaire businessman; a High Court judge ruled he could still inherit from the family's £14.5 million trust
articles.summary: A judge at the High Court of England and Wales has ruled that a man could inherit from a £14.5 million family trust despite DNA evidence establishing that
articles.body: A judge at the High Court of England and Wales has ruled that a man could inherit from a £14.5 million family trust despite DNA evidence establishing that he was not the biological son of the millionaire businessman who created it. The dispute arose between two brothers raised together within the same family, after one challenged the other's right to benefit from the trust. Although the court accepted that the younger brother was not biologically related to their father, it concluded that the circumstances surrounding the trust's creation supported his continued inclusion as a beneficiary, according to Ellisons' account of the judgment.How DNA evidence challenged a brother's £14.5 million trust inheritanceThe case, Marcus v Marcus [2024] EWHC 2086 (Ch), concerned Jonathan Marcus and Edward Marcus, who were raised as brothers by Stuart and Patricia Marcus. Stuart was a successful businessman who founded a toy business in 1962, which later acquired Sequin Art.Both brothers worked within the family business, which subsequently separated into two groups of companies. Their connection to the business also became central to a family trust established by Stuart to protect his assets and provide for his descendants.According to Ellisons, which represented Edward in the proceedings, Stuart transferred shares in the family companies into a discretionary trust in 2003. The trust was created for his children, with assets worth approximately £14.5 million becoming the subject of the dispute.The disagreement eventually placed the meaning of the trust's wording at the centre of a High Court inheritance battle.One brother challenged the other's place in the trustThe dispute followed the discovery that Patricia had had an affair. Jonathan subsequently argued that Edward should not be entitled to benefit from the trust because he was not Stuart's biological child.The claim sought to exclude Edward from the discretionary trust, potentially removing him from consideration when trustees decided who should receive its assets.Edward argued that he was Stuart’s son, and secondly that the trust documents should be interpreted in a way that even if he was not Stuart’s biological son, he should still be included.The legal issue was not simply whether Edward had Stuart's DNA, according to Ellisons. The court also had to consider what Stuart intended when he created the trust and whether the term children and remoter issue was intended to include Edward. That distinction became decisive in the judgment.What did the judge decide about Edward's biological fatherThe judge found that Edward was not Stuart's biological son. DNA evidence therefore resolved one part of the dispute against him.But the finding did not automatically decide whether he could remain a beneficiary. The court took into account the circumstances in which Edward and Jonathan had grown up and Stuart's view of his family at the time he created the trust.Both brothers had been born to Stuart and Patricia while they were married and had been raised as their children. The judge also took into account that when the trust was created Stuart believed Edward was his son.Ellisons said in a summary of the judgment that there was no evidence that Stuart believed he had any other biological children apart from Jonathan and Edward. Nor was there any evidence to indicate that he intended to treat the brothers differently in establishing the trust.How did the High Court interpret the family's trust documentsThe central issue was how the word children should be understood in Stuart's settlement. Ordinarily, the term would refer to biological children, unless the document or its surrounding circumstances supported a broader interpretation.In his judgment dated 16 August 2024, Master Marsh examined the trust's language alongside the circumstances in which Stuart had established it. The judge considered the family's background, the purpose of the settlement and Stuart's understanding of his relationships at the time.The settlement had been established when Stuart and Patricia had been married for around 30 years. Their sons were already in their early twenties, and there was little likelihood of Stuart having additional children. The judge also found no reason for Stuart to favour one brother over the other when setting up the arrangement.Why the court rejected a narrow interpretation of childrenThe judge recognised that the trust's wording did not expressly identify Edward and Jonathan by name. Instead, it referred to the children and remoter issue of the settlor, leaving the class of beneficiaries open to future additions.However, the court considered that the circumstances surrounding the settlement were sufficiently clear to establish whom Stuart intended to include.Master Marsh decided that a reasonable person aware of the relevant background would understand Stuart to have meant Edward and Jonathan when referring to his children. The wording was not intended to mean Edward and Jonathan only if they were biologically related to him.The judge also considered the difference that a narrow interpretation would produce between Stuart's settlement and Patricia's separate trust, which was established in materially similar terms. Because Patricia was Edward's biological mother, he would remain a beneficiary of her settlement even if excluded from Stuart's.The court found that such unequal treatment would be inconsistent with the circumstances in which the two arrangements had been created.What did the £14.5 million trust containThe settlement was established on 29 November 2003, with Stuart transferring shares in the family companies to its trustees.By the time of the proceedings, the trust held substantial shareholdings in Kitfix Investments Ltd and Kitfix Swallow Group Ltd. According to the High Court judgment, the assets included 1,094,536 A shares and 1,499,623 B shares in Kitfix Investments Ltd, alongside 1,338,972 shares in Kitfix Swallow Group Ltd.The combined value of those holdings was estimated at approximately £14.5 million.The trust was discretionary, meaning its beneficiaries did not automatically receive fixed shares of its assets. Instead, the trustees had powers to distribute income or provide benefits to one or more people within the eligible class. It preserved his eligibility to benefit from the trust, rather than giving him an automatic entitlement to a defined portion of its value.The High Court's decision meant Jonathan's attempt to exclude Edward from Stuart's settlement failed. The judge ruled in Edward's favour on the central question concerning the meaning of the trust's wording.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Iran’s Northern Fleet Commander Rear Admiral Mohsen Razzaqi has warned US forces in the region against any aggression, saying coordination among the
articles.body: Iran’s Northern Fleet Commander Rear Admiral Mohsen Razzaqi has warned US forces in the region against any aggression, saying coordination among the country’s armed forces is at its highest level and naval units remain prepared to defend its maritime borders round the clock.Speaking at a ceremony in the northern coastal city of Astara, Razzaqi described human resources as the most important asset of the army navy. He said naval forces, including missile and drone units as well as commandos, maintain a continuous presence to protect Iran’s waters.“The cost of any aggression against Iran must be raised to such an extent that the enemy will no longer dare attack the country again,” he said, according to the IRNA news agency.Razzaqi said Iran’s military strategy extends beyond simply bringing hostilities to an end and focuses on imposing prohibitive costs on any aggressor. He cited the country's missile, drone and naval capabilities, strategic geographical position and the steadfastness of its people as key elements of its deterrence strategy.His remarks come amid a series of warnings from Iranian officials and military commanders signalling the country's preparedness to respond to any renewed aggression.Earlier, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei warned the US in a post on X, saying: “Start a war, and you’ll face a devastating response.”In late October, Iran's Supreme leader Ayatollah Sayyid Mojtaba Khamenei ordered “maximum deterrence”, directing military commanders to ensure an immediate and effective response, without geographical restrictions, in the event of another attack on the country.The directive also called for maintaining intelligent combat readiness to decisively counter threats and continuously updating target banks.The latest warning from Tehran comes after the US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced the formation of a new task force to disrupt Iran's alleged use of land transit routes to transport advanced weapons, dual-use technologies and other sanctioned materials.According to a CENTCOM statement, Task Force Iron Gate was established on Saturday under the direction of CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper. The task force will comprise approximately 20 civilian and military personnel based in Tampa, Florida.It will coordinate with other US government agencies to prevent the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illicit revenue streams across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea, as Washington seeks to tighten restrictions on Tehran's military supply networks.You use AI every day. articles.title: Chained to bed, windows covered in foil: How ex-husband held US woman captive for 2 years
articles.summary: A woman in Fargo, North Dakota, was rescued after allegedly being chained to a bed for two years, beaten and sexually assaulted by her ex-husband and his
articles.body: A woman in Fargo, North Dakota, was rescued after allegedly being chained to a bed for two years, beaten and sexually assaulted by her ex-husband and his girlfriend, police said. The woman was found after a maintenance worker heard her cries for help at an apartment complex on November 3.Officers responding to the building found her restrained by a heavy chain and padlock around her right ankle, with the chain secured to the bedframe, according to court documents cited by the New York Post.A maintenance technician had reported hearing muffled screams from the apartment, prompting the building management to call 911.The victim was taken to hospital after being freed. Police interviewed her with the help of a translator, as she communicated through a translation app, according to the reports.Her ex-husband, 40-year-old Arturo Calzada-Becerril, and his girlfriend, 41-year-old Erendira Amoles, have been charged in connection with the case.Woman allegedly brought from Mexico and held captiveAccording to court documents cited by Valley News Live, the woman told investigators that Calzada-Becerril brought her to Fargo from Mexico in 2024 and kept her confined in the apartment, where she was not allowed to leave.The bedroom reportedly had a security camera pointed towards the bed, while its windows were covered with aluminium foil. The woman said she was given food twice a day and forced to use a bucket beside the bed as a toilet.Investigators found bruising on her arms, legs and face. She also told police that Calzada-Becerril and Amoles had beaten and sexually assaulted her. She said she had been punched, leaving a scar on her forehead.An investigative report cited by Inforum described the restraints as chains secured to the bed's headboard and footboard with large bolts, washers and nuts. The chains were covered with foam pool noodles and secured with Master Lock padlocks.Court documents state that Calzada-Becerril told police he kept the woman restrained so that "she did not run away", claiming she was addicted to drugs and that he did not want her to start using again.Prosecutors alleged that the pair held the woman captive to obtain immigration status. The victim is an American citizen, according to Valley News Live.Two accused face kidnapping chargesCalzada-Becerril and Amoles made their first court appearance on Friday, November 6. Both have been charged with kidnapping, along with additional counts including domestic violence and assault, Valley News Live reported.A judge set bail at $500,000 each. Prosecutors said both defendants could face deportation. Additional charges may be filed as the investigation continues.According to court documents, Amoles was usually responsible for handling the victim and unlocking her from the bedframe. She returned to the apartment with her eight-year-old daughter shortly after authorities discovered the woman.Neighbours shocked by discoveryResidents of the apartment complex said they were stunned to learn that a woman had allegedly been held captive in the building for two years without their knowledge.Erin Schauer, a resident, told Valley News Live that security personnel regularly patrolled the complex."We have security coming through from like 6 to 11 p.m. every single night. They stop in the hallways, they walk through every single building, they drive around," she said."That is really scary. You hear about that all the time on the news, but the fact that it was literally right over there," she added.Another resident, Reed Bertsch, said he could not understand how nobody had suspected what was happening."It's unbelievable. I just can't believe no one heard it, or you know, had any suspicion of something like that going on," he said.A longtime tenant also told Valley News Live that she had noticed the foil covering the apartment windows for years but had not known why it was there.Fargo police are working with the Cass County State's Attorney's Office as the case proceeds, according to Valley News Live.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi celebrated Diwali with security personnel deployed in Chhattisgarh's Bastar region on Sunday.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi celebrated Diwali with security personnel deployed in Chhattisgarh's Bastar region on Sunday. PM Modi credited the forces for their sacrifices in the fight against Left-wing extremism and took a dig at previous Congress governments, accusing them of failing to tackle the insurgency."Because of your sacrifices we have put an end to the terror of Naxalism here," PM Modi said while addressing the personnel.Addressing the gathering, PM Modi said he had come to celebrate the festival with the security personnel as a representative of the country's 140 crore citizens.Drawing a parallel between the responsibilities of soldiers guarding India's borders and security personnel fighting insurgency within the country, PM Modi said internal security was equally important for protecting the nation's unity and integrity."When a nation's internal security is strong, external enemies cannot succeed. However, when internal security is weakened, external enemies also begin to raise their heads," he said.The prime minister then turned his attention to the previous Congress-led governments, alleging that they had treated Naxalism as an incurable problem rather than taking decisive action against it."If you look at the figures from 2004 to 2013, you will find that every year, the number of our brave soldiers martyred was higher than the number of Naxalites killed. Unfortunately, the governments of that time treated Naxalism as an incurable disease and left it unaddressed," he said.Recalling the violence that had gripped Chhattisgarh for years, PM Modi cited the 2010 Dantewada attacks, in which 76 CRPF personnel were killed in an encounter with Naxalites and 44 civilians lost their lives in another incident."This land was soaked in the blood of our brave soldiers. But not a single voice of anguish was heard from those influential leaders living in their palaces. Not a single tear was shed by them," he said.The prime minister also spoke about his tradition of celebrating Diwali with security personnel, saying they were like family to him. He recalled previous celebrations with the forces, from Kargil and Lepcha in the Himalayas to Sir Creek and INS Vikrant.Bastar has remained at the centre of the government's campaign against Left-wing extremism, with the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) and Chhattisgarh Police playing a key role in anti-Naxal operations.On March 31, the government announced that the country had been freed from the menace of Naxalism following the elimination of several senior leaders and cadres, alongside the surrender of hundreds of others.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Why mandarin ducks are popping up across the West Midlands
articles.summary: Expert say the birds are now an increasingly common sight, with numbers continuing to rise.
articles.body:
With vibrant colours and bright orange sail feathers, mandarin ducks have recently been popping up across the West Midlands, delighting residents and leaving many wondering how such a striking species ended up on their doorstep.

The exotic-looking birds have been attracting birdwatchers and photographers to a number of beauty spots across the region, including Birmingham's Sutton Park.

One local photographer, Jamil El Farsi, said finding the birds so close to home was "unbelievable".

"They don't look real, they look like a painting," he said. "That's how vibrant they are, the colours."

Native to East Asia, mandarin ducks were introduced to England from China in the early 20th Century and have since become naturalised, with populations appearing mainly in south-east England, as well as parts of Wales and Scotland.

The ducks were considered non-invasive and posed no threat to native species, remaining a "rare and special sight", said the Canal and River Trust.

The males are best known for their colourful sail feathers, while the females have grey-brown feathers and a white eye stripe.

With their distinctive appearance, some social media users have even mistaken the birds for images generated by artificial intelligence (AI).

El Farsi, who captured a series of striking images, described how he spent hours waiting to take the perfect shot of the birds, which tend to favour quieter areas and can sometimes be challenging to photograph.

The birds, which are known for nesting in holes in old trees, are often found hiding beneath overhanging willows.

"They are very shy birds and they tend to hide," El Farsi, from Birmingham, explained.

He said of photographing one bird: "I was waiting honestly for about two hours for it because it was swimming around one of the logs, just to perch on one of the logs, so you could get a portrait, like a picture of it out of the water."

The birds have continued to attract attention from visitors and wildlife enthusiasts, with crowds visiting Sutton Park with their phones and cameras in the hopes of spotting them.

El Farsi, who first saw the birds in The Leasowes in Halesowen, returned to Sutton Park in October with his wife and children to see them again.

"People were coming from everywhere, Wolverhampton [and] all around the Midlands," he said.

"As soon as we got there, my younger kids were running around. And as soon as they saw them, they were jumping around: 'Oh, they're still here, they're still here, dad'."

Wildlife experts said mandarin ducks were now an increasingly common sight in Britain, with numbers continuing to rise in recent years.

There were now "far more of them" in the West Midlands, explained Nathan Cope, founder of BirdFact.

"Around Birmingham, they now turn up about five times as often in birdwatchers' records as they did 10 years ago, even though the number of people recording birds has stayed about the same," he said.

Cope told the BBC the British population of mandarin ducks was thought to have grown from birds that had escaped from collections about a century ago.

"Numbers across the UK have grown more than sixfold since the mid-1990s and spread through central England, so the West Midlands is catching up with the south," he added.

The Birmingham and Black Country Wildlife Trust said the species had thrived in England, with breeding numbers increasing by 663% between 1995 and 2024.

There are now thought to be between 4,400 and 7,000 breeding pairs in the UK.

James Benwell, from the trust, said he believed mandarin ducks were the "world's most beautiful duck".

"The males are truly exotic looking, with bright colours and their distinctive sail feathers. The females are far less showy," he said.

The trust said there had been a resident population at Sutton Park for a number of years, as well as a long-term resident at Perry Hall Park and sightings at Sandwell Valley, Red House Park Pool and Fens Pools.

Benwell said autumn was the best time to spot mandarin ducks because the males regained the "distinctive" and "dramatic" plumage they had lost during the summer moulting season.

"It's a really good time to go out and spot them now, and the population at Sutton Park has taken up residence on the popular Keeper's Pool, meaning that they are delighting many visitors to the park," Benwell said.

"There are around 15 males present, as well as more females, so they really are a wonderful sight to behold and it's well worth making a trip to see them."

articles.title: This Diwali, Gen Z is lighting up the ‘No’ button! Read Full Story
articles.summary: This Diwali, Gen Z is redefining the festival by rejecting material excess and embracing meaningful celebrations, mindful shopping, and thoughtful gifting, while prioritizing their well-being over societal expectations.
articles.body: From buying outfits that will make exactly one appearance to attending parties out of sheer FOMO, the youngsters is pressing the unfollow button on festive-season excess. This Diwali, the goal is to spend less, stress less and stop treating celebrations like a full-time job. Diwali is the season of lights, laddoos and the sudden realisation that you have absolutely nothing to wear. Add a few expensive gifts, a shopping cart full of things you didn’t know you needed and a social calendar that would exhaust a celebrity on a promotional tour, and you have the modern festive-season checklist. Here is what young people are leaving behind this festive season.But Gen Z is beginning to ask an important question: What if we just... didn’t?Unnecessary shopping? Unfollow. Performative gifting? Unfollow. Attending a party because you saw everyone else’s Instagram stories? Hard pass. The idea isn’t to cancel Diwali but to cancel the pressure to make it look like the most spectacular festival ever celebrated. “I believe festivals should be about celebrating in ways that feel meaningful to us, rather than keeping up with what everyone else is doing. You don’t need new clothes, expensive gifts or a big party to make the festival special,” says Shishir R, a 27-year-old business owner.Rewear the outfit, not the anxietyApparently, repeating an outfit is still considered a crime in some festive circles. Gen Z, however, is beginning to embrace the art of the repeat. After all, if celebrities can rewear outfits, why should the rest of us behave as though our clothes have an expiry date? “I don’t understand why repeating an outfit has to be a big deal. I’ll happily wear the same lehenga again and style it differently. I’d rather spend on an experience I enjoy than buy clothes I’ll probably wear only once,” says a 23-year-old student, Siya Doshi.Add to cart, then reconsider!Festive discounts have a special talent for convincing us that spending ₹5,000 to save ₹500 is an act of financial genius. But mindful shopping is gaining ground among young consumers, who are learning to distinguish between wanting something and being manipulated by a countdown timer. The new strategy is simple: pause before purchasing, check the wardrobe before shopping and remember that a discount isn’t a personal invitation. “I’ve started asking myself whether I’d buy something if it weren’t discounted. If the answer is no, I probably don’t need it. I still love shopping for festivals, but I don’t want to end up with things I bought impulsively and will regret later,” says Sia Joshi (28), an engineer.Gifting, not financial planningDiwali gifting is lovely until you realise that a casual exchange of presents has turned into an unofficial economic summit. The youngsters is increasingly questioning the need to spend beyond its means just to prove affection. Thoughtful presents, handwritten notes and homemade treats can be just as meaningful. “I’d rather receive something small that shows a person knows me well than an expensive gift bought just because it’s Diwali,” says Anya Godambe, a 21-year-old makeup artist.Your absence isn’t a national emergencyThe festive social calendar can be relentless. One house party, two family dinners, three friends’ get-togethers and an office celebration that everyone is attending because attendance has apparently become a personality trait. Worse is the FOMO. You decline one invitation, open Instagram and discover that everyone is having the time of their lives without you. Gen Z is learning that being everywhere isn’t the same as enjoying anything. Sometimes, the best Diwali plan involves staying home, eating something delicious and not having to shout over music to hold a conversation. “I don’t feel the need to attend every party just because everyone else is going. Sometimes, I’d rather spend the evening with my family, eat good food and relax. Saying no doesn’t mean I don’t care about my friends; it just means I want to enjoy the festival without exhausting myself,” says Ayan Gupta (24), a gamer by profession.Ziana Kasnavia, 14-year-old student, says, "I’d rather have someone help me clean the house because it’s something I really hate doing. That way, I can spend more time going out and chilling with my friends."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: When the smoke settles, what remains? The unseen health and environmental risks
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Festivals in India bring people together through lights, colours, music, food and community celebrations.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Festivals in India bring people together through lights, colours, music, food and community celebrations. From bursting firecrackers and decorating homes to playing with colours, organising processions and gathering along riverbanks, festivities are an integral part of the country's social and cultural life. But as celebrations grow in scale, so does their environmental footprint.The pollution generated during festivals is often discussed in isolation, particularly when air quality deteriorates after Diwali. However, the environmental impact of celebrations goes much further. Firecrackers release particulate matter into the atmosphere, synthetic colours can introduce chemicals into water bodies, large gatherings generate plastic waste, and loud music and fireworks contribute to noise pollution.These effects are not confined to a particular festival or community. Across different celebrations, the use of disposable materials, increased consumption, transportation, decorative lighting and improper waste disposal can put additional pressure on the environment.The consequences can extend beyond the days of festivities, affecting public health, urban sanitation, water quality and local ecosystems. In cities already struggling with vehicle emissions, industrial pollution, construction dust and untreated waste, the additional burden can make environmental management more challenging.So, what happens to the environment when millions of people celebrate simultaneously, and how do these activities affect our everyday lives?Diwali and the science of air pollutionDiwali is among the occasions when the relationship between celebrations and air pollution becomes particularly visible. Firecrackers release a mixture of gases, suspended particles and chemical compounds into the atmosphere. Their emissions include particulate matter such as PM2.5 and PM10, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. Depending on their composition, fireworks can also release metallic compounds, including barium and aluminium.The concern is particularly around PM2.5, particles measuring 2.5 micrometres or less. These particles are small enough to penetrate deep into the lungs, reaching the alveoli, the tiny air sacs where oxygen enters the bloodstream. Some components of particulate pollution can also enter the bloodstream and trigger inflammation.Dr Abhishek Agrawal, Medical Officer at a government hospital, explains how exposure to firecracker emissions can affect respiratory health."During festivals like Diwali, the concentration of pollutants in the air can increase due to firecracker emissions. People inhale these pollutants, particularly fine particulate matter, which can enter deep into the lungs and cause irritation and inflammation of the respiratory tract. We often see people complaining of coughing, throat irritation, breathlessness and worsening respiratory symptoms during periods of poor air quality."The impact is not uniform across the population. Children, elderly people and individuals with pre-existing respiratory conditions are particularly vulnerable to sudden changes in air quality."Children, elderly people and individuals suffering from asthma, COPD or other respiratory conditions are particularly vulnerable. Their respiratory systems may not be able to cope with sudden exposure to high levels of pollution. Even people who do not have a pre-existing respiratory illness can experience discomfort, especially when pollution levels remain elevated for several hours," Agrawal said.The problem can also continue after the celebrations end. During the post-monsoon period, low wind speeds, atmospheric stability and temperature inversions can prevent pollutants from dispersing quickly. When firecracker emissions combine with existing sources such as vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions and construction dust, pollution levels can remain elevated."The effects of pollution do not necessarily disappear once the firecrackers stop. Fine particles can remain suspended in the atmosphere, depending on weather conditions. People may continue experiencing coughing, throat irritation, wheezing and breathing difficulties in the following days. Those with existing respiratory conditions should be especially cautious," Agrawal added.Beyond the lungs: How festive pollution affects multiple organsAir pollution is not merely a respiratory concern. Exposure to particulate matter, chemical emissions and excessive noise can affect several organs, including the heart, brain and nervous system.While the lungs are the first point of contact for inhaled pollutants, fine particles can trigger inflammatory responses that affect other parts of the body. Air pollution has been associated with increased blood pressure, disturbances in heart rhythm and a higher risk of cardiovascular complications, particularly among people with existing heart conditions."The impact of festive pollution is not limited to the lungs. Fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, can penetrate deep into the alveoli and trigger oxidative stress and inflammation. This can lead to coughing, wheezing, breathlessness and asthma attacks. Air pollution can also increase blood pressure, disturb heart rhythms and trigger cardiovascular complications, including heart attacks, in vulnerable individuals," Agrawal explained.The brain and nervous system can also be affected. Exposure to polluted air and excessive noise can contribute to headaches, dizziness, stress and sleep disturbances. Prolonged exposure to air pollution has also been associated with adverse effects on cognitive health.Chemical exposure presents another concern. Certain toxic metals and chemical residues released by fireworks and other festive materials can pose risks to organs such as the kidneys and liver, depending on the substance, concentration and duration of exposure.Noise pollution adds another dimension to the health burden. Sudden, high-intensity sounds from firecrackers can cause tinnitus, temporary hearing discomfort and, at sufficiently high exposure levels, permanent hearing damage.Can a few hours of festive pollution cause lasting health problems?One of the common misconceptions about festive pollution is that its effects are limited to the duration of celebrations. However, even short-term exposure to high concentrations of pollutants can trigger health complications, particularly among vulnerable individuals.People with asthma may experience sudden attacks, while those with existing respiratory or cardiovascular conditions may develop breathing difficulties or other complications. Repeated exposure over time can increase the risk of chronic health problems."Even a few hours of exposure to high levels of pollution can trigger asthma attacks, breathing difficulties and cardiovascular complications in vulnerable individuals. Repeated exposure increases the risk of long-term health problems. The duration of symptoms varies depending on the level of exposure and the person's health. Some people may recover within a few hours, while others may continue experiencing symptoms for several days," Agrawal said.The effects can also be reflected in healthcare demand. Indian studies examining air pollution during and after Diwali have reported increases in respiratory complaints, hospital visits and admissions, particularly involving asthma exacerbations and breathing difficulties."Studies in India have reported an increase in respiratory hospital visits and admissions following Diwali, particularly involving asthma attacks, breathing difficulties and other respiratory complaints. Hospitals and healthcare facilities also deal with cases involving burns, eye injuries and hearing-related problems during festive periods," Agrawal said.The environmental footprint of celebrationsWhile air pollution receives considerable attention, other forms of environmental degradation often go unnoticed during festivals.The use of synthetic colours during celebrations, for instance, can create problems for water bodies and soil. Some commercially available colours may contain chemical compounds and heavy metals that can cause skin irritation, allergic reactions and eye problems. When washed away, these substances can enter drainage systems and eventually reach rivers, lakes and other water bodies.Similarly, religious offerings, flowers, plastic packaging and decorative materials discarded during large gatherings can add to water and land pollution. Idol immersion activities involving plaster of Paris, synthetic paints and non-biodegradable decorations can further increase the waste entering lakes and rivers.The consequences are particularly concerning in urban areas where water bodies are already under pressure from untreated sewage, industrial discharge and solid waste. Additional festive waste can worsen existing contamination and affect aquatic ecosystems.Large public celebrations and processions also generate considerable quantities of disposable plates, plastic bottles, food packaging and other materials. When waste is not segregated or collected properly, it can clog drains, accumulate in public spaces and eventually enter nearby water bodies.The problem does not end with the celebrations. Municipal sanitation workers are often left to clear large quantities of discarded materials, firecracker remnants, food waste and plastic packaging. Improper disposal and open burning of collected waste can further contribute to local pollution.Noise pollution: The impact beyond what we can seeAnother dimension of festive pollution is noise, which can affect people even when there is no visible deterioration in air quality.Firecrackers, loudspeakers, musical processions and public celebrations can expose residential neighbourhoods to excessive sound levels. Sudden explosions and prolonged exposure to loud music can interfere with sleep, concentration and everyday routines.Repeated exposure to excessive noise can also contribute to stress, anxiety and hearing-related problems. People with cardiovascular conditions, infants, elderly residents and patients recovering from illnesses may be particularly affected by disturbances during late-night celebrations.The impact extends to animals and urban wildlife. Pets can experience distress due to sudden loud noises, while birds and other species may alter their movement and behaviour in response to repeated disturbances.The World Health Organization has associated excessive environmental noise with sleep disturbance, hearing impairment and cardiovascular health risks. This makes noise pollution an important public health concern rather than merely an inconvenience during celebrations.The hidden burden of electricity consumption and festive shoppingModern celebrations also involve a considerable increase in consumption. Decorative lighting across homes, markets and commercial establishments increases electricity demand, while shopping, gift packaging, food deliveries and travel add to energy use and waste generation.Although LED lights consume less electricity than conventional lighting, their widespread use across residential and commercial areas can still contribute to higher cumulative demand.Excessive artificial lighting also contributes to light pollution, which can interfere with the natural day-night cycles of birds, insects and other wildlife. For nocturnal species, artificial illumination can affect navigation, feeding and other behavioural patterns.The growing use of plastic decorations, disposable utensils, thermocol, synthetic materials and packaging creates another challenge. Much of this waste is used for a limited period before being discarded, adding to the burden on already stretched municipal waste-management systems.These individual activities may appear relatively small, but their combined impact across densely populated cities can be considerable.Why the effects can last beyond the festivitiesOne of the reasons festive pollution becomes a concern is that the environmental impact does not always end when celebrations stop.Airborne particles can remain suspended depending on weather conditions, while chemical residues and improperly disposed materials can continue affecting soil and water quality. Waste accumulated in drainage systems can also create problems during subsequent rainfall.The extent of pollution depends on several factors, including the scale of celebrations, the materials used, local environmental conditions and the efficiency of waste collection and disposal.It is also important to distinguish between pollution generated during festivals and the wider pollution crisis. Festivals are not the sole reason behind deteriorating air or water quality. Instead, they can add concentrated emissions and waste to an environment already dealing with multiple sources of contamination.This cumulative impact also raises questions about environmental inequality. A person celebrating indoors may have limited exposure to pollution, while a street vendor, traffic policeman, delivery worker or sanitation worker may remain exposed for several hours. Similarly, children and people with existing health conditions may face greater health risks than others.Can celebrations become more environmentally responsible?Reducing festive pollution does not mean giving up celebrations. It requires greater awareness of how everyday choices during these occasions affect the environment.Using natural colours, opting for traditional clay idols, avoiding single-use plastics, segregating waste and ensuring that religious offerings are disposed of responsibly can help reduce the burden on water bodies and public spaces. Community celebrations, designated immersion facilities and better waste collection can also improve environmental management.Individual precautions are equally important, particularly during periods of poor air quality. Agrawal recommends avoiding areas with heavy firecracker smoke, limiting outdoor activities when pollution levels are high and taking measures to reduce indoor exposure."People should avoid unnecessary outdoor activities when air quality is poor, particularly during early morning and late evening hours if pollution levels are elevated. Patients with asthma should follow their prescribed medication and treatment plans. Children and elderly people should limit exposure to smoke and avoid areas where firecrackers are being burst."He also recommends wearing a well-fitted N95 mask when outdoor exposure to particulate pollution cannot be avoided, keeping windows closed during periods of heavy pollution and using HEPA air purifiers indoors, if available. Outdoor exercise should be avoided when pollution levels are high. Firecracker residues should be cleaned using damp methods rather than dry sweeping, which can resuspend particles in the air.People experiencing persistent breathlessness, wheezing or chest pain should seek medical attention rather than dismissing the symptoms as temporary festive discomfort.Ultimately, the environmental cost of celebrations cannot be measured only by the pollution recorded on a particular day. It must also account for the waste left behind, the pressure on natural resources and the health implications for people who continue to live and work in these surroundings.Festivals are an important part of India's cultural and social fabric.
